name: Louis Zamperini
tagline: The man who refused to be broken
story:
In the summer of 1943, Louis Zamperini's B-24 bomber crashed into the Pacific Ocean. Of the eleven crew members, only three survived the impact. Stranded on a tiny life raft with no food and no water, the former Olympic distance runner — who had once shaken Adolf Hitler's hand at the 1936 Berlin Games — began the longest endurance race of his life.

For forty-seven days, Zamperini and his pilot Russell Allen Phillips drifted across two thousand miles of open ocean. They fought off sharks that circled constantly, caught rainwater in their mouths, and ate raw fish and albatross. When Japanese planes strafed their raft with bullets, Zamperini dove into shark-infested waters and clung to the underside. By the time they washed ashore on the Marshall Islands, they were skeletal — Louis had dropped from 150 pounds to barely 80.

But survival at sea was only the prologue. Captured by the Japanese, Zamperini was sent to a series of POW camps where a sadistic guard known as 'The Bird' singled him out for daily beatings and psychological torture. The Bird forced other prisoners to punch Zamperini in the face, one after another, for hours. He was starved, humiliated, and told he would never go home. For over two years, every day was designed to destroy him.

He came home. He came home broken, haunted by nightmares, spiraling into alcoholism — but he came home. And then, slowly, impossibly, he rebuilt. Zamperini returned to Japan decades later and publicly forgave his captors, including The Bird. He ran a leg of the Olympic torch relay through Nagano in 1998, at age 81, past the site of one of his prison camps. Some people survive. Zamperini chose to live.
